### Loading the packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse) 
library(readxl)
```

### Importing the data

```{r}
Height_Data_Raw <- 
  read_excel("Oak Data Entry MCRS Field Trip.xlsx", 
             sheet = "Seedling Heights")

Moist_Data_Raw <- 
  read_excel("Oak Data Entry MCRS Field Trip.xlsx", 
             sheet = "Soil Moisture")

SPAD_Data_Raw <- 
  read_excel("Oak Data Entry MCRS Field Trip.xlsx", 
             sheet = "SPAD", 
             na = "NA")
```

## Cleaning Data Set

\*\*I examined and cleaned the data all in one chunk

You may be either examining `SPAD_Data_Raw`, `Height_Data_Raw`, `LICOR_Data_Raw`, or `Moist_Data_Raw` for your ANOVA question. Examine your data set using the diagnostic functions I've given you above in the How to Examine and Clean Data section.

```{r}
view(Moist_Data_Raw)
#view it in separate window
nrow(Moist_Data_Raw)
#how many rows
dim(Moist_Data_Raw)
#number of rows and columns respectively
glimpse(Moist_Data_Raw)
#glimpse of the data, too complicated! 

ncol(Moist_Data_Raw)
#how many columns
str(Moist_Data_Raw)
#looking at it all...
names(Moist_Data_Raw)
#looking at all names of columns
moistdataclean<-
  Moist_Data_Raw |> 
  select(Date, Treatment, VWC1_perc, VWC2_perc, VWC3_perc) |> 
  na.omit() |> 
  arrange(Date, Treatment) |> 
  mutate(vwc1 = as.numeric(VWC1_perc)) |> 
  mutate(vwc2= as.numeric(VWC2_perc)) |> 
  mutate(vwc3= as.numeric(VWC3_perc)) |> 
  mutate(date=as.character.Date(Date))
# making a new dataframe called moistdataclean where I only display date, treatment, and the three vwc values
# getting rid of the nas in the data frame
#arranging the data by date and treatment 
#renaming some of my data columns to be more simple, along with changing their formats (percentages to numerical values and dates to categorical )
?select
#looking at the select function and what it does 
moistdatacleaner<-
  moistdataclean |> 
  select(!c(VWC1_perc,VWC2_perc,VWC3_perc)) |> 
  select(!(Date))
#making a new data frame called moistdatacleaner and removing the original untidy columns
moistdatacleaner
#viewing the new dataframe
moistdataanova<-
  na.omit(moistdatacleaner) |> 
  mutate(avg.moisture=((vwc1+vwc2+vwc3)/3)) |> 
  select(!c(vwc1,vwc2,vwc3)) |> 
  mutate(avgmoisture=round(avg.moisture,3)) |> 
  select(!(avg.moisture)) |> 
  mutate(date=case_when(
    date=="2026-10-21" ~ "2026-10-15", 
    date!="2026-10-21"~date
  ))

#making a new dataframe called moistdataanova
#removing NAs 
# calculating the average of the moisture percentages, adding it to the table, and removing the three separate observations
#rounding the averages, adding it to the table, and removing the unrounded version
#big big fix- date said 10.21, supposed to be 10.15, i changed it to what it should be
typeof(moistdataanova$avg.moisture)
typeof(moistdataanova$date)
typeof(moistdataanova$avgmoisture)
view(moistdataanova)
summary(moistdataanova$avgmoisture)
#looking into the types of data each column is
# viewing the dataframe in a new window
#summarizing the moisture column to see if there are any outstanding outliers




?replace

```

```{r}
# View data set
view(SPAD_Data_Raw)
#viewing the raw data frame 
spaddataclean<-
  SPAD_Data_Raw |> 
  select(Date, Treatment, Leaf1, Leaf2, Leaf3, Leaf4, Leaf5, Leaf6) |> 
  na.omit() |> 
  arrange(Date, Treatment) |> 
  mutate(date=as.character.Date(Date)) |> 
  select(!(Date))
#making a new dataframe selecting only date, treatment, and the SPAD values by leaf
#removing the NAs
#arranging the data by date and treatment
#changing the date column to be categorical
#removing the old date column
spaddataclean
#visualiZing new dataframe
spaddatareg<-
  na.omit(spaddataclean) |> 
  mutate(avg.spad=((Leaf1+Leaf2+Leaf3+Leaf4+Leaf5+Leaf6)/6)) |> 
  select(!c(Leaf1, Leaf2, Leaf3, Leaf4, Leaf5, Leaf6)) |> 
  mutate(avgspad=round(avg.spad,3)) |> 
  select(!(avg.spad)) |> 
  filter(avgspad>=10) |> 
  left_join(moistdataanova) |> 
  na.omit()
#making a new dataframe called spaddatareg for the regression work
#removing NAs from the dataframe
#calculating the average of all SPAD values and adding it to the table as a column called avg.spad
#removing the individual leaf SPAD values I used to make the calculations
#rounding the avg SPAD values and removing the unrounded SPAD averages
#filtering out any SPAD averages less than zero because the summary function below showed me that I had two SPAD averages under 10; when checking the notes in the raw data, these low values came from brown leaves, so I removed the values 
#adding the moistdataanova dataframe 
#removing the NAs once more
view(spaddatareg) 
#viewing the new data frame
summary(spaddatareg$avgspad)
##two outliers that i need to remove
#this is where I checked for outliers, they will no longer show because i removed them, thats a good thing!
```

## Exploratory Data analysis (from previous Assignment)

```{r}
moistdataanova |>   
  ggplot()+   
  aes(x=avgmoisture)+   
  geom_histogram() 
#histogram to visualize avg soil moisture, there doesnt seem to be any major outliers
```

```{r}
moistdataanova
#looking at my dataframe
moistdatabp<-
  moistdataanova|> 
  ggplot() + 
  aes(x=Treatment,
      y=avgmoisture, fill=date)+
  labs(title = "Average Soil Moisture by Treatment and Date",
       y = "Average Soil Moisture in percentage", x = "Treatment")+
  geom_boxplot()
#making a boxplot and calling it moistdatabp
#using treatment for x and avg moisture for y
#titling it and labeling axes
moistdatabp
#visualizing the figure
```

[some interpretations]{.underline}

- [There seems to be little to no data for natural recruits]{.underline}

- [soil moisture seems to have a lot lower averages on the 8th than on the 15th, there was some rain between these two days, so this could be the reason- can look into it deeper with tests of differences later]{.underline}

- [Dead Tree seemed to have some of the highest soil moistures]{.underline}

- [Adult canopy seemed to have lower soil moisture on the 15th compared to Dead Tree and Open Space, which is not what I was expecting considering open space has no shade (i thought those numbers would be the lowest)- this could also be looked into deeper with tests of differences later]{.underline}

```{r}
spaddatareg |>    
  ggplot()+   
  aes(x=avgspad)+   
  geom_histogram() 
#histogram for the avg spad values, there doesnt seem to be any more major outliers because i filtered out values under 10
```

```{r}
spaddatareg
hist(spaddatareg$avgspad)
hist(spaddatareg$avgmoisture)
#looks pretty normal
spadmoist <- lm(avgspad~avgmoisture, data=spaddatareg)
plot(spadmoist)
#QQ plot shows it is normal 
summary(spadmoist)
#look at coefficients, the speed estimated std. is the slope of the line
slope <- coef(spadmoist)[2]
#2 is in brackets to say i only want the second one in the series, doesnt provide intercept value
slope
#slope is -0.224
int <- coef(spadmoist)[1]
#1 is in brackets- viceversa to say i only want the first value in the series, doesnt provide slope/speed
int
#intercept is 34.50514
summary(spadmoist)$coefficients[2,4]
#very very small
Rsq <- summary(spadmoist)$r.squared
Rsq
#0.16, not that good of a correlation, not close to 1



spaddatasp<-
  spaddatareg|> 
  ggplot() + 
  aes(x=avgmoisture,
      y=avgspad, color=Treatment)+
  ylim(0,40)+
  xlim(0,3)+
  labs(       y = "Average SPAD value", x = "Average Soil Moisture in Percentage")+
  geom_point()
#making a plot and calling it spaddatasp
#using moisture as x and spad as y
#using color to indicate treatment
#setting a domain and range
#labelling axes
spaddatasp
#visualizing plot
```

[some interpretations]{.underline}

- [There seems to be much less data for natural recruits again]{.underline}

- [From a visual standpoint, there is no outstanding trend, this could be because of the very low r squared value, meaning the soil moisture and SPAD value are not strongly correlated]{.underline}

- [Dead Tree data seems to be clustured at very low soil moistures and very high soil moistures, there are not many points in the middle]{.underline}

- [Natural Recruits and open space have the lowest SPAD values compared to the other microhabitats]{.underline}

- [Adult canopy seems to have very little data as well, only 4 points]{.underline}
